title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) measuring whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the fraction of validator‑passing vendor‑specific CLI configurations produced from operator intent, relative to direct LLM generation. Tasks were a curated multi‑vendor (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) intent manifest; a deterministic validator encoded syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic routing‑reachability, and destructive‑pattern checks; and the declared model snapshot was gpt-5-mini. Under the preregistered paired design (shared initial candidate per task), every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 300/300, guarded = 300/300; n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). Because the guarded arm invoked zero repair calls, the preregistered single‑repair policy was not exercised and no repair‑success diagnostics are observed. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the 300‑task manifest, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being proposed for intent→configuration translation in NetOps; operators commonly mitigate risk with validators and constrained repair loops. We asked: does a deterministic validate‑and‑(single)‑repair intervention measurably increase the probability that an LLM’s vendor CLI candidate passes an operational validator, compared with direct use of the initial generation? We preregistered a paired binary design (study_id study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e) and executed it end‑to‑end under the frozen master prompt (artifact: provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Our manuscript reports the preregistered analysis and artifact‑anchored diagnostics.
sections.related_work: Closely related work covers intent‑driven configuration with LLMs, generate–validate architectures, and NetOps validators. Representative references used for positioning and method choices include an intent→configuration study (Nguyen Tu et al., 2024), recent CNSM/NetOps LLM configuration proposals (Chakraborty et al., 2024; Mondal et al., 2025), deterministic policy verification for routing (Weitz et al., 2016), and benchmarks for LLM→network tasks (NetLLMBench, 2024). We cite these verified sources to justify our paired, validator‑centered confirmatory design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered (ID and full plan hashed: preregistration SHA‑256 a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6) and executed exactly as specified. Design: paired binary outcomes on n=300 tasks. For each task a single initial candidate was generated (shared across arms). Baseline outcome = validator(initial_candidate). Guarded outcome = validator(initial_candidate) OR validator(repair_candidate) where a single automatic repair call is allowed if the validator rejects the initial candidate. Task manifest and validator. The curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest and per‑task payloads (intent, initial_state, required_sequence, difficulty tags) are published (artifact path: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The deterministic validator used throughout is recorded in the execution artifacts and referenced by id in scoring traces as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0); validator outputs and traces are embedded in execution/scoring/*.json (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json). Prompts, repair templates, and transformation metadata are published in the transformation manifest and model configuration (execution/transformation_manifest.json SHA‑256 = ef4f9a7e6e5e67398eca449221f29490ff0a107c38e2fd07cf833f9c35e4971a; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). These artifacts contain the adapter family, prompt template identifiers, and the declared model snapshot (gpt-5-mini). Execution. The run invoked only the preregistered shared initial generation stage for each task (300 model calls total; maximum_model_calls per preregistration = 600). All provider calls, raw responses, validator runs, and logs were recorded and hash‑signed (see execution_manifest/artifact_hashes). Analysis. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided; 95% CI via paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Secondary pre‑specified per‑vendor paired comparisons are Bonferroni‑controlled; repair diagnostics were pre‑specified as exploratory conditional on initial failures. Missingness, retries, and contamination. The preregistered retry policy and contamination checks were executed and logged (see execution/execution_log.jsonl and analysis/contamination_summary.csv). All artifacts and hashes are published for independent verification.

sections.discussion: Meaning of the result. The preregistered confirmatory test observed a ceiling effect: the declared model snapshot and prompt regime produced initial candidates that satisfied the deterministic validator for every curated task. Under this condition the bounded guarded policy (single automatic repair) could not change outcomes; the trial therefore provides a valid, artifact‑anchored null/ceiling observation for this exact experiment, but it does not imply that G‑V‑R is unnecessary in general. Operational regimes where G‑V‑R adds value. A nontrivial marginal safety benefit from G‑V‑R requires (i) a nonzero initial failure rate for the chosen generator/prompt/model snapshot, or (ii) a validator that captures dynamic/timing hazards or deeper routing semantics that the generator is likely to violate. Practical implications. Teams deploying G‑V‑R should (a) instrument and measure initial generation failure rates for their chosen prompt/model/task distribution, (b) align validator fidelity (static rule set vs simulation/emulation) with the class of harms of operational concern, and (c) choose repair budgets (single vs iterative repair) based on measured failure severity and repairability. Reproducible follow‑ups. To bound where G‑V‑R helps, future runs should increase manifest hardness (adversarial or out‑of‑distribution tasks), expand validator scope (simulators/Batfish‑style dynamic checks), test multiple model families and snapshots, and permit multi‑step repair policies. Artifact availability. All artifacts required to reproduce the run are published and hash‑signed: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 6d99060659a7...b3), execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 ef4f9a7e6e5e...), execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 1acce92558ed...), execution/scoring/*.json (examples above), execution/responses/* (raw generator outputs), execution/provider_calls/* (provider traces), and analysis/* (analysis artifacts and logs). The deterministic validator is referenced consistently in scoring traces as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0); its rule set and implementation are included in the published artifact bundle (see execution/transformation_manifest.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl for exact file identifiers).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory evaluation of a bounded G‑V‑R policy on a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest. Under the declared model snapshot, prompt regime, and deterministic validator, every initial candidate passed the validator and the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked; hence no marginal improvement was observed. The study highlights that the operational benefit of G‑V‑R is conditional on the generator error rate, validator coverage, and task hardness. We publish complete artifacts and hashes to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary these axes.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, forbidden destructive patterns) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; manifest design and the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.

Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) intentionally fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measurement of generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
